ABSTRACT Detecting collusion rings in modern banking requires modeling the evolving structural interactions among heterogeneous entities (customers, accounts, and devices) rather than isolated transaction features. Most graph-based fraud detectors assume abundant labels, yet confirmed fraud labels in anti-money laundering (AML) settings routinely arrive months after the fact. We introduce Audit-HCL , a dynamic heterogeneous graph neural network framework that uses dual-view contrastive learning to operate effectively under this label scarcity. Audit-HCL represents the transaction ecosystem as a temporal sequence of heterogeneous graph snapshots, encodes them through a metapath-guided heterogeneous attention encoder, and tracks evolving node behavior with a GRU-based temporal dynamics module. A cross-view contrastive objective aligns structural and temporal perspectives for legitimate nodes while separating anomalous ones, guided by an anomaly-aware negative sampling strategy. Experiments on two public benchmarks (Elliptic and IBM AML-Synthetic) show that Audit-HCL outperforms fourteen baselines by 3.2% in AUC-ROC and 6.8% in F1-score, with the gains over the strongest competitors confirmed by paired significance tests, and that it retains useful discriminative power with zero fraud labels. On the synthetic IBM AML benchmark, it also detects laundering patterns an average of 7.4 weeks ahead of confirmed events ( 2 . 3 × the lead time of the best baseline) by capturing gradual structural drift before large-scale fund transfers begin, although the magnitude of this lead time is tied to the controlled typologies of the synthetic data and should be read as indicative rather than as a guarantee for production AML environments.
Introduction The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime estimates that between two and five percent of global GDP is laundered annually 1 . A particularly damaging form is collusive fraud : coordinated networks of accounts that route funds through layered transactions to conceal their origin. Traditional rule-based anti-money laundering (AML) systems are interpretable but rely on fixed thresholds and pattern templates that adversaries defeat through structural obfuscation
2
. Graph neural networks (GNNs) address fraud detection by modeling transactions as relational structures 3–5 , and GNN-based detectors have demonstrated an ability to capture the relational camouflage strategies used by fraudsters 6,7 . Three persistent challenges, however, limit their applicability to collusive AML. Banking networks are inherently heterogeneous: customers, accounts, and devices participate in transactions through semantically distinct relation types, and homogeneous GNNs that collapse this diversity onto a single flat graph discard the discriminative signals encoded in cross-type interaction patterns 8,9 . Collusion rings are also not static structures. Mule accounts are recruited incrementally, transaction corridors are established over weeks, and the eventual burst of fund transfers is preceded by a prolonged period of gradual structural change that no single graph snapshot can capture 10,11 . Compounding both challenges is the scarcity of supervision: confirmed fraud labels in AML investigations typically arrive months after the suspicious activity, leaving the labeled fraction of any training corpus small and unrepresentative of evolving attack patterns
7,12
. Prior work addresses each challenge individually. Heterogeneous GNNs such as HAN 8 and HGT 9 handle entity diversity but assume static topologies. Temporal graph models including EvolveGCN 10 and TGN 13 capture dynamics but treat all nodes as the same type. Self-supervised methods like GraphCL 14 and GRACE 15 reduce label dependence but operate on homogeneous, static graphs. No existing method handles all three challenges together. We propose Audit-HCL ( Audit -oriented H eterogeneous C ontrastive L earning), a dynamic heterogeneous graph neural network framework that addresses all three challenges jointly. Our contributions are: ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS

• We formalize collusive fraud detection on dynamic heterogeneous graphs and introduce a metapath-guided heterogeneous attention encoder (MGHA) that captures cross-type interaction patterns along semantically meaningful relation paths.
• We design a GRU-based temporal dynamics module (TDM) that tracks how entity representations evolve across graph snapshots, enabling explicit detection of structural drift in mule account networks.
• We propose a dual-view contrastive objective with anomaly-aware negative sampling that exploits both structural and temporal perspectives without requiring fraud labels during pre-training.
• Experiments on two public benchmarks show 3.2% average AUC improvement, effective zero-label operation, and 7.4-week average earlier detection (2 . 3 × the lead time of the best baseline) over existing methods. Section reviews related work; Section describes the framework; Section presents experiments (RQ1–RQ6, and scalability); Section concludes.

sections.name: Related Work (1/2)
sections.text:
Graph Neural Networks for Fraud Detection Weber et al. 2 first applied graph convolutional networks to the Elliptic Bitcoin dataset, establishing GNNs as a viable approach for financial fraud detection. CARE-GNN 6 added a reinforcement learning module to filter camouflaged neighbors that fraudsters place near legitimate users. PC-GNN 7 tackled severe class imbalance through a label-balanced neighbor sampler and distance-weighted aggregation. On the heterogeneous side, Johannessen et al. 16 applied heterogeneous GNNs to multi-entity AML networks; Cheng et al. 17 surveyed the broader landscape. Beyond graph-based approaches, Jiang et al. 18 provided a systematic review of deep learning architectures for sequential decision-making in financial systems, demonstrating that models designed to capture temporal dependencies consistently outperform static counterparts across fraud detection and risk management tasks. The broader value of architectures tailored to difficult, structurally complex inputs is also visible outside finance: Duan et al. 19 propose DSYOLO, a dynamic snake convolution segmentation model that adapts its receptive field to elongated, irregular crack morphologies under heavy background interference, showing that input-aware structural inductive biases improve robustness in challenging environments. Our metapath-guided attention pursues an analogous goal in the graph setting, shaping aggregation around fraud-relevant relational structure rather than treating all connections uniformly. Most of these methods assume static graph structures and require substantial labeled data, two conditions that rarely hold in practice.
Heterogeneous Graph Representation Learning Heterogeneous information networks encode multiple node and edge types, retaining semantic signals that homogeneous projections lose. HAN 8 introduced hierarchical attention over metapath-based neighbors for type-aware aggregation; HGT 9 generalized the Transformer to heterogeneous graphs with type-dependent attention heads; R-GCN 20 used relation-specific weight matrices for knowledge graph completion. In the self-supervised setting, HeCo 21 contrasted network schema and metapath views, while SHGP 22 used metapath structure for heterogeneous graph pre-training. All of these methods operate on static snapshots and do not model how entity behavior changes over time.
Dynamic and Temporal Graph Learning Temporal graph methods split into discrete-time and continuous-time approaches. In the discrete setting, EvolveGCN 10 uses an RNN to evolve GCN parameters across snapshots, while DySAT 23 combines structural and temporal self-attention. Continuous-time methods TGAT 11 and TGN 13 process event streams with temporal encoding. The TGB 2.0 benchmark 24 standardized evaluation for temporal heterogeneous graphs and found that many methods struggle when both heterogeneity and dynamics are present. Han et al. 25 introduced a symmetry-aware deep learning framework that exploits balance and invariance properties inherent in financial records, significantly improving credit risk prediction robustness under severe class imbalance. SEHTGNN 26 (NeurIPS 2025) proposed an efficient architecture for heterogeneous temporal graphs but targeted link prediction rather than anomaly detection. Our work combines temporal modeling with heterogeneous attention for fraud specifically. Chen et al. 27 combined a temporal Transformer with a conditional tabular GAN for credit card fraud detection, showing that sequential modeling of transaction histories paired with synthetic oversampling of minority fraud instances yields substantial gains on heavily imbalanced datasets.
Contrastive and Self-Supervised Learning on Graphs Graph contrastive learning has advanced self-supervised representation on graphs considerably. GraphCL 14 studied augmen- tation strategies for contrastive pre-training; GRACE 15 introduced adaptive augmentation for node-level learning; DGI 28 maximized mutual information between local patches and global summaries; MVGRL 29 contrasted representations across / ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS

Figure 1. Overview of the Audit-HCL framework. Raw banking transactions are organized into a temporal sequence of heterogeneous graph snapshots. The Metapath-Guided Heterogeneous Attention encoder (MGHA) produces type-aware node embeddings at each timestep, which the Temporal Dynamics Module (TDM) aggregates across snapshots via gated recurrent
units. Dual-view contrastive learning aligns structural and temporal perspectives, and the anomaly scoring module combines
contrastive deviation with structural drift for final fraud prediction. diffusion-augmented views. For AML, LaundroGraph 12 applied self-supervised graph learning but used a homogeneous construction. Lo et al. 30 proposed Inspection-L for money laundering detection via self-supervised node classification. Jin et al. 31 (IJCAI 2025) argued that standard graph augmentations can destroy anomalous structural signals, precisely the signals most useful for fraud detection. Our anomaly-aware negative sampling is designed to preserve and exploit those signals during contrastive optimization. Audit-HCL is deliberately assembled from components that have individually proven effective, and we do not claim that metapath attention, gated recurrent temporal aggregation, or InfoNCE-style contrast are new in isolation. The two-level intra/inter-metapath attention in MGHA follows the design popularized by HAN 8 , and the GRU temporal aggregation in TDM is a standard recurrent encoder 32 . Three aspects distinguish our method from this prior work. First, the contrastive objective aligns a structural view against a temporal view of the same node, rather than two structural augmentations of a static graph as in GraphCL 14 , GRACE 15 , or HeCo 21 ; the temporal branch supplies a second view that static heterogeneous contrastive methods do not have. Second, the anomaly-aware negative sampler in Eq. (13) intentionally retains and up-weights the structurally inconsistent nodes that conventional augmentation pipelines tend to smooth away, directly targeting the failure mode that Jin et al. 31 identify for contrastive anomaly detection. Third, we treat heterogeneity, temporality, and label scarcity as a single objective and derive a dual anomaly score (contrastive deviation plus structural drift) that ties the learned representation to an interpretable, deployable signal. The contribution therefore lies less in any single module than in the specific way the temporal and structural views are made to interact under label-free supervision; the ablation in Section quantifies how much of the gain comes from this interaction rather than from the modules individually.
The Audit-HCL Framework Fig. 1 illustrates the Audit-HCL architecture, which has four components: (1) dynamic heterogeneous graph construction, (2) a metapath-guided heterogeneous attention encoder, (3) a temporal dynamics module, and (4) a dual-view contrastive objective with anomaly scoring.

sections.name: Experiments
sections.text:
We address six research questions:
• RQ1: Does Audit-HCL outperform state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised methods?
• RQ2: How much does each component (MGHA, TDM, dual-view contrastive learning, anomaly-aware negatives) contribute?
• RQ3: Can Audit-HCL detect laundering patterns earlier than existing approaches?
• RQ4: How does Audit-HCL perform under varying levels of label availability?
• RQ5: How sensitive is performance to key hyperparameters, and how does it scale with graph size?
• RQ6: How robust is Audit-HCL to label noise and snapshot granularity, and how can its anomaly scores be interpreted in practice?
Datasets
We evaluate on two public benchmarks that provide diverse financial fraud scenarios at scale. Elliptic 2 . A Bitcoin transaction network containing 203,769 nodes and 234,355 edges across 49 temporal snapshots. Each node has 166 features derived from transaction metadata. Approximately 2% of nodes are labeled as illicit, 21% as licit, and the remainder are unlabeled. The fraud ratio reported as 2.0% in Table 1 is computed over the entire node set (illicit nodes divided by all nodes, including the unlabeled majority). Computed over the labeled subset only (the ≈ 23% of nodes that carry a licit or illicit label), the illicit fraction is ≈ 8.7%; we report the all-node figure for consistency with the IBM AML statistics, where labels are dense. We distinguish direct transfer links from multi-hop flow paths to form heterogeneous edges. IBM AML-Synthetic 34 . A large-scale synthetic dataset designed to mimic real-world money laundering patterns, including fan-in, fan-out, and circular flow typologies. It contains 5.2 million transactions across 500K accounts over 12 months. We construct weekly snapshots (52 total) with three node types (sender, receiver, intermediary) and four edge types.
Table 1 summarizes key statistics.
/ ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS

Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Construction Because neither benchmark is distributed in the dynamic heterogeneous format our model consumes, we describe the conversion in full. The generic schema of the Problem Formulation ( { Customer , Account , Device } with four relations) is the union template; each dataset instantiates the subset of types its raw fields support, which is why | A | and | R | differ across the two benchmarks in Table 1. Feature preprocessing. For both datasets, continuous node features are standardized to zero mean and unit variance per dimension. To avoid temporal leakage, the standardization statistics (and any threshold used for typing, below) are estimated only from snapshots in the training split and then applied to all snapshots. Categorical fields (e.g., payment format, currency) are one-hot encoded. Unlabeled nodes are retained for message passing and contrastive pre-training but excluded from the supervised fine-tuning loss. Elliptic. The raw data provide one node type (transaction) with 166 features and one directed payment relation over 49 native time steps, which we use directly as snapshots. We derive a two-type, three-relation heterogeneous schema as follows. Nodes are typed by transactional role: transactions whose out-degree exceeds the 90th percentile within a snapshot are promoted to a relay role and the remainder keep the transaction role ( | A | = 2 ). Edges are typed into (i) direct_transfer , the native one-hop payment links; (ii) multi_hop_flow , materialized between a transaction and the transactions reachable two hops downstream along a directed payment path, capturing layering corridors; and (iii) temporal_coref , linking the same wallet’s transactions across adjacent snapshots ( | R | = 3 ). Metapaths P
1 and P
2 are instantiated over { transaction , relay }; the device-based path P
3
is inactive on Elliptic, which has no device information. IBM AML-Synthetic. The raw data are a transaction log (5.2M transactions over 500K accounts, each with timestamp, sender, receiver, amount, currency, and payment format), with transaction-level laundering labels. We aggregate transactions into 52 weekly windows. Within each window, accounts become nodes and are typed by their dominant role: sender (predominant out-flow), receiver (predominant in-flow), or intermediary (substantial in- and out-flow, i.e., receive- and-forward behavior), giving | A | = 3 . Per-account window features are computed from the log: in/out transaction counts, in/out amount sums and dispersion, number of distinct counterparties, currency mix, and mean inter-transaction interval. Edges are the directed transfers between accounts, typed into four relations by transfer characteristics ( | R | = 4 ): standard , large_value (amount above the training-window 95th percentile), cross_currency , and pass_through (a received amount forwarded within the same window). A node-level laundering label is set positive if the account participates in any transaction the generator marks as laundering within the observation horizon. Reproducibility. All thresholds (out-degree percentile for relay typing, large-value percentile, pass-through window) are fixed before training from training-split statistics and listed above so the construction can be reproduced exactly; the conversion scripts operate deterministically given a fixed train/validation/test temporal split.

Main Results (RQ1) Table 2 and Fig. 2 report results across both datasets. Audit-HCL achieves 95.3% AUC on Elliptic and 92.4% on IBM AML, surpassing the best baseline (LaundroGraph) by 3.2 and 3.5 percentage points respectively. Three observations stand out. First, heterogeneous methods (HAN, HGT) consistently outperform their homogeneous counterparts by 2–4% AUC. Notably, HGT gains only 0.8% over HAN on Elliptic despite its more expressive transformer architecture, which suggests that the choice of metapath relation types matters more than attention expressivity in this setting. Second, temporal methods (TGAT, TGN) improve over static heterogeneous models by roughly 1–1.5% AUC on both datasets. TGN outperforms EvolveGCN on both benchmarks, consistent with its use of node memory modules rather than parameter- level recurrent updates; EvolveGCN’s GCN parameter evolution appears less stable under the sparse labeled regime. Third, among self-supervised methods, GRACE lags behind LaundroGraph by 2.5% AUC on Elliptic, likely because homogeneous augmentation destroys the edge-type distinctions that are informative for fraud subgraphs. The P@100 metric is arguably the most operationally relevant figure for compliance teams with limited review capacity. Audit-HCL achieves 87.4 on Elliptic versus 80.2 for LaundroGraph, a 9% relative gain that translates directly into fewer false positives at the top of the alert queue. On IBM AML the margin is similarly substantial (81.6 versus 74.4). Comparing against the best fully supervised baseline, PC-GNN reaches only 79.4 on Elliptic despite using all available labels, 8 points below / ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS

Because several gaps over the two closest competitors are small relative to the seed-level spread, we test them directly rather than relying on non-overlapping means. The five runs use a shared set of random seeds, so we treat the per-seed scores as paired and apply a paired t -test (df = 4 ); we additionally report a seed-level bootstrap (20,000 resamples) 95% confidence interval on the mean gap. On Elliptic AUC, Audit-HCL improves over LaundroGraph by 3 . 2 points (95% CI [ 2 . 7 , 3 . 7 ] , t = 18 . 6 , p < 0 . 001 ) and over PC-GNN by 3 . 8 points (95% CI [ 3 . 3 , 4 . 3 ] , p < 0 . 001 ). On IBM AML AUC the gaps are 3 . 5 points over LaundroGraph (95% CI [ 3 . 1 , 3 . 9 ] , p < 0 . 001 ) and 4 . 1 points over PC-GNN (95% CI [ 3 . 7 , 4 . 5 ] , p < 0 . 001 ). The F1 improvements are larger and likewise significant ( p < 0 . 001 for all four comparisons; smallest gap 6 . 8 points). Every 95% confidence interval excludes zero by a margin substantially larger than the combined seed variance, so the improvements are not attributable to seed-to-seed variation. We note that these tests are computed on only five seeds, so the confidence intervals should be read as indicative; the consistency of the sign and magnitude of the gap across seeds, datasets, and metrics is the stronger evidence.
Ablation Study (RQ2) We evaluate four ablated variants on both Elliptic and IBM AML. In w/o MGHA, the metapath-guided attention encoder is replaced with a standard GAT that aggregates over all edge types without distinguishing relation semantics. In w/o TDM, the GRU temporal module is removed and only the final snapshot embedding is used for scoring. In w/o Dual-View, a single structural view replaces the cross-view contrastive objective. In w/o AN-Neg, anomaly-aware negative sampling is replaced with uniform random sampling. Removing MGHA produces the largest drops on both datasets: 2.6 AUC points on Elliptic and 2.8 on IBM AML, with F1 falling by 4.3 and 4.7 points respectively. The disproportionately large F1 loss relative to AUC suggests that MGHA is especially critical for correctly ranking borderline nodes near the fraud/legitimate decision boundary, not merely for coarse score separation. TDM contributes the second-largest gain, and its benefit is notably stronger on IBM AML, where the 52-week snapshot sequence captures more of the gradual behavioral drift that characterizes fan-out laundering. Summing the individual drops gives totals of roughly 8.0 points on both datasets, which exceeds the full model’s lead over LaundroGraph (3.2 and 3.5 points). This non-additivity suggests positive interactions among components: the temporal representations from TDM, for instance, are more useful as the structural view anchor in the contrastive objective than static snapshots would be.
Early Detection Analysis (RQ3) We define the Early Detection Rate (EDR@ ∆ t ) as the fraction of eventually-confirmed laundering nodes that the model ranks in the top-500 anomaly scores at least ∆ t weeks before the confirmed event. Audit-HCL maintains higher EDR at every lead time, and the margin over LaundroGraph widens as the horizon extends: from 7.5 percentage points at ∆ t = 2 to 12.2 points at ∆ t = 10 (Table 4, Fig. 4b). At ∆ t = 8 weeks, Audit-HCL detects 42.1% of laundering nodes compared to 28.5% for LaundroGraph, a 47.7% relative gain. The growing advantage at longer lead times reflects the contribution of the structural drift score s
d
( v ) : drift accumulates over several weeks as fan-out source accounts progressively establish transfer corridors, providing a signal that contrastive methods without temporal modeling cannot capture at short horizons. The rapid decay in PC-GNN’s EDR beyond ∆ t = 4 weeks (dropping from 51.2% to 20.8%) is particularly telling: without temporal context, supervised detection depends on structural patterns that simply are not present weeks before the main laundering event. Across the IBM AML typology instances, Audit-HCL issues alerts an average of 7.4 weeks before confirmed events, compared to 3.2 weeks for the best baseline, a 2 . 3 × improvement in actionable lead time.
Label Efficiency (RQ4) A key practical advantage of Audit-HCL is that its contrastive pre-training requires no fraud labels. We evaluate performance as a function of the labeled data fraction available for downstream classification. Fig. 5 shows that label availability affects the four methods quite differently. PC-GNN and TGN lose 15–20 AUC points when the label fraction drops below 1%, making them unreliable in the early-deployment scenario that motivates this work. LaundroGraph is more robust because its contrastive pre-training provides a reasonable initialization regardless of label count, but it still gains approximately 12 points between 0% and 10% labels on Elliptic. Audit-HCL gains only 7.9 points over the same range, and its zero-label performance of 87.4% on Elliptic already exceeds both PC-GNN and TGN at label fractions up to roughly 3–5%, which corresponds to the window during which a newly deployed AML system is accumulating confirmed cases through active investigations. The gap between Audit-HCL and LaundroGraph at zero labels is substantial on both datasets (7.2 points on Elliptic, 7.2 points on IBM AML), but narrows to 3.2 and 3.5 points at 10% labels. This compression suggests that Audit-HCL’s temporal and heterogeneous structural features transfer more effectively to the downstream classifier / ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS

Sensitivity Analysis (RQ5) We examine sensitivity to four hyperparameters on Elliptic: the anomaly score trade-off λ , contrastive temperature τ , temporal window w , and edge dropout rate p
e
. The anomaly trade-off weight λ (Fig. 6a) peaks at λ = 0 . 6 (95.3% AUC) and degrades on both ends: removing the drift term entirely ( λ = 0 . 0 ) costs 3.5 points, while suppressing it completely ( λ = 1 . 0 ) costs 1.4 points. The asymmetry confirms that contrastive deviation is the primary discriminator, but structural drift contributes non-redundant information, particularly the gradual ramp during the Layering phase that contrastive signals alone cannot resolve at that stage. The contrastive temperature τ (Fig. 6b) is forgiving in the range [ 0 . 05 , 0 . 10 ] , where AUC varies by less than 0.5 points. Increasing beyond 0.2 softens the negative-sample repulsion and allows fraudulent accounts to collapse into the legitimate cluster, costing 1.5 points by τ = 0 . 5 . The temporal window w (Fig. 6c) shows diminishing returns: each additional snapshot from w = 1 to w = 4 adds roughly 0.5 points, but the gain from w = 4 to w = 8 is only 0.3 points total, a poor trade against the twofold memory increase. Edge dropout p
e (Fig. 6d) follows a clear optimum at 0.3: at lower rates the model overfits the observed graph topology, while rates above 0.4 begin removing metapath-critical edges and degrade AUC by up to 3.1 points at p
e
= 0 . 7 . Across all four hyperparameters, default values remain within 0.5 points of the optimal, indicating that the model is not unusually sensitive to tuning.

Scalability Analysis We evaluate training time and GPU memory as a function of graph size by sub-sampling IBM AML to five scale points (10K–500K nodes). As shown in Fig. 7, Audit-HCL scales near-linearly in both time and memory. At 500K nodes it requires 35.2 GB and 56.4 s/epoch, approximately 57% of TGN’s memory footprint and 58% of its per-epoch time. HGT runs out of memory at that scale, while TGN fits but at a steeper super-linear trajectory (Fig. 7b). The efficiency advantage is most pronounced at large scales: at 200K nodes, Audit-HCL already uses 14.6 GB versus TGN’s 31.2 GB, a 2.1 × reduction. This makes Audit-HCL the only method among the three to operate within a single A100 80 GB GPU across all tested scales and the most practical choice for financial institutions whose transaction graphs routinely exceed 100K active accounts per monitoring window.
Robustness and Interpretability (RQ6) High-stakes AML deployment exposes a model to imperfect labels and to design choices such as snapshot length. We probe two such factors and then discuss how the anomaly scores are read in practice. To make the comparison concrete, Table 5 reports both Audit-HCL and the two closest competitors (PC-GNN and LaundroGraph) under each perturbation, with the clean/default-setting value from Table 2 reproduced in the leftmost column so that the drop in parentheses is directly comparable across methods. Label noise. We corrupt a fraction η of the fine-tuning labels by random flipping on Elliptic (10% labeled fraction) and measure test AUC. The drop grows roughly quadratically with η for every method, which is the expected behavior for a binary classification head exposed to symmetric label flips, but the slope differs sharply. The fully supervised PC-GNN loses 9 . 3 points by η = 20% because its representation and its classifier are trained jointly on the corrupted labels; the self-supervised LaundroGraph, which decouples representation learning from labels, loses 6 . 2 points; and Audit-HCL retains 92 . 3% AUC at η = 20% for a drop of only 3 . 0 points. The mechanism is that the label-free contrastive pre-training, together with the structural drift score s
d
( v ) that is computed without any labels at all, fixes most of the representation before any label is seen, so flipped labels only perturb the lightweight classification head rather than the encoder. The relative ordering (Audit-HCL < LaundroGraph < PC-GNN in degradation) is preserved at every noise level, which makes the robustness gain attributable to the training paradigm rather than to a single noise rate. Snapshot granularity. On IBM AML we rebuild the dynamic graph at monthly (12 snapshots), bi-weekly (26), and the default weekly (52) resolution, and rerun all three methods end-to-end. Finer granularity helps every method, but with diminishing returns: each method recovers most of its weekly performance already at the bi-weekly setting, so the principal cost of a coarse snapshot is incurred between monthly and bi-weekly resolution. Coarser snapshots blur the gradual structural drift that TDM exploits and, on the baselines that lack an explicit temporal module, blur the only signal those models receive about behavioral change. Audit-HCL nonetheless degrades least in absolute terms ( − 2 . 1 points at monthly vs. − 3 . 1 for PC-GNN and − 2 . 9 for LaundroGraph), and the ordering at each granularity matches the ordering in the clean default. The model is therefore sensitive to granularity in a predictable direction rather than brittle, and weekly windows are a reasonable default for the laundering typologies considered. Interpreting the scores. The two components of s ( v ) map onto distinct analyst-facing questions. The structural drift score s
d
( v ) answers “how unusually is this account’s local graph position changing over time?” and is monotonic, so accounts can be ranked and the contribution of each snapshot inspected as the per-step terms d
t
v of Eq. (8) . The contrastive deviation score s
c
( v ) answers “how inconsistent are this account’s structural and temporal behaviors?” and tends to sharpen only once a pattern is behaviorally unambiguous. In a triage workflow the drift term provides an early, soft flag while the deviation term provides a later, high-confidence one; reporting both, rather than a single fused number, lets an analyst see why an account surfaced. We caution that these scores are association signals, not determinations of wrongdoing, and are intended to prioritize human review / ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS

Discussion The ablation results make a direct case for joint modeling. Removing any one of heterogeneity-awareness, temporal dynamics, or contrastive self-supervision pushes performance below the strongest single-paradigm baseline (PC-GNN or LaundroGraph), and the joint removal of any two components degrades AUC by 7–10 points. This is not a story of one dominant module carrying the others. MGHA captures relational diversity that homogeneous encoders cannot resolve; TDM encodes the behavioral trajectory that static representations miss; and contrastive learning separates fraud accounts from the legitimate majority without requiring labeled fraud examples. The three challenges are largely orthogonal, so treating them as separate engineering sub-problems, rather than addressing all three in a single model, consistently leaves performance on the table. Audit-HCL reaches 87.4% AUC on Elliptic with zero fraud labels, which suggests it can surface candidate alerts for human review before an investigation pipeline has produced confirmed ground truth, rather than serving as a stand-alone decision system. Inference on IBM AML averages 1.1 seconds per weekly snapshot on a single GPU, which is compa

tible with standard AML batch processing cycles, and the scalability analysis confirms the model stays within a single A100 80 GB GPU up to 500K active accounts. We frame these as evidence of practical feasibility on the benchmarks studied; true deployment suitability additionally depends on factors our public-data experiments cannot measure, including concept drift in live fraud typologies, label-confirmation latency, and institution-specific data quality, which we return to below. Several limitations warrant attention. First, the early-detection results (RQ3) are obtained entirely on IBM AML-Synthetic, whose laundering typologies are generated from known templates with relatively clean phase structure; the 7.4-week average lead time should therefore be read as evidence that the model can exploit gradual structural drift when such drift exists in the data , not as a calibrated forecast of lead time in production systems, where laundering patterns are noisier, partially observed, and adversarially adapted. Quantifying this gap requires labeled real-world AML data that, for confidentiality reasons, is rarely public, and closing it is an important direction we cannot settle with current benchmarks. The metapath set must be defined by a domain expert, and performance is contingent on this manual choice: an incomplete or poorly chosen metapath set caps what relational patterns MGHA can detect, and the device-based path is simply unavailable on datasets such as Elliptic. Automated metapath discovery for financial transaction graphs is an open problem that we did not address here. The anomaly threshold requires either a small labeled validation set or manual calibration before deployment. Finally, snapshot discretization introduces a temporal granularity floor: patterns that unfold within a single snapshot window are invisible to TDM, and continuous-time models may be better suited to that regime. We also note that both benchmarks, including the real-but-pseudonymous Elliptic data, differ from a live banking environment in scale, feature richness, and label-confirmation dynamics, so the absolute numbers reported here are best interpreted comparatively (across methods) rather than as expected production performance. Adapting Audit-HCL to continuous-time event streams and removing the manual metapath requirement are the natural next steps.

Conclusion We presented Audit-HCL, a dynamic heterogeneous graph neural network framework that addresses entity heterogeneity, temporal dynamics, and label scarcity jointly. Metapath-guided heterogeneous attention, GRU-based temporal modeling, and dual-view contrastive learning with anomaly-aware negatives combine to produce node representations that separate fraudulent behavior from legitimate activity without fraud labels at training time. Across two public benchmarks (Elliptic and IBM AML-Synthetic), Audit-HCL outperforms fourteen baselines by an average of 3.2% AUC and 6.8% F1, with the gains over the closest competitors confirmed by paired significance tests, achieves 87.4% AUC on Elliptic with zero fraud labels, and , on the synthetic IBM AML benchmark, detects laundering patterns an average of 7.4 weeks ahead of confirmed events, 2 . 3 × the lead time of the best baseline. Scalability analysis confirms near-linear time and memory growth up to 500K nodes. The results indicate that self-supervised temporal heterogeneous graph learning is a promising direction for the label scarcity and structural complexity of AML, while validation on live, real-world AML data, automated metapath discovery, and continuous-time modeling remain necessary steps before the approach can be relied upon in production.
